items.title: Pneumoperitoneum on standing x-ray
items.contentHtml:
Pneumoperitoneum in standing x-ray

  • Pneumoperitoneum visible as subdiaphragmatic air in standing x-ray (chest or abdomen) is detected in 70-80% of peptic ulcer perforations; its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • The standing radiograph should be taken with the patient standing at least 10 minutes beforehand to allow free air migration.
  • If the patient cannot stand, left lateral decubitus with horizontal ray (Hampton projection) is an alternative; air accumulates between the liver and the costal wall.
  • Examination trap: in contained perforation or covered by omentum, pneumoperitoneum may be absent; CT scan is more sensitive.

items.foco: Sudden pain in epigastrium on table
items.title: Sudden pain in epigastrium
items.contentHtml:
Sudden pain in the epigastrium

  • The sudden pain in the epigastrium of sudden onset, described as shooting or stabbing, is the classic symptom of peptic ulcer perforation; It usually occurs at table or during activity, not necessarily postprandial.
  • The pain is initially localized in the epigastrium and then generalizes to the entire abdomen due to chemical peritonitis; Radiation to the shoulder (Kehr sign) suggests diaphragmatic irritation. In sudden pain, the differential diagnosis includes acute pancreatitis, acute cholecystitis, perforated appendicitis and mesenteric ischemia; the history of ulcer or use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs guides.
  • Perforation is the second most common complication of peptic ulcer, after hemorrhage; The most common location is the anterior surface of the duodenal bulb.

items.title: Jobert's sign
items.contentHtml:
Jobert's sign

  • The Jobert sign consists of abolished hepatic dullness on percussion in the right upper quadrant, due to the interposition of free air between the liver and the abdominal wall.
  • It is a classic finding of pneumoperitoneum due to perforation of the hollow viscus, but it has low sensitivity and may be absent in perforations small or covered.
  • Abolished hepatic dullness is evaluated by percussing from the mammillary level downwards in the right midclavicular line; replacement by tympanism suggests air.
  • On physical examination, Jobert's sign is associated with other signs of peritonitis such as flat abdomen and decompression pain; Its presence requires imaging confirmation.

items.title: Abdomen in plank
items.contentHtml:
Abdomen in plank

  • The abdomen in plank is the involuntary and sustained muscular contracture of the abdominal wall, secondary to chemical peritonitis due to spillage of gastric acid into the peritoneal cavity.
  • It presents as generalized rigidity, with pain on palpation and rebound pain (Blumberg sign); The contracture is more intense in the upper quadrants.
  • The muscle contracture is a viscerosomatic reflex response; Its absence in the elderly or immunocompromised does not rule out peritonitis (atypical presentation).
  • The flat abdomen with sudden pain in the epigastrium and pneumoperitoneum constitutes the classic triad of peptic ulcer perforation; Emergency surgery is indicated.

items.foco: Chemical peritonitis due to gastric acid
items.title: Chemical peritonitis
items.contentHtml:
Chemical peritonitis due to gastric acid

  • Chemical peritonitis is produced by the action of gastric acid and pepsin on the peritoneum; it is initially sterile, but after 6-12 hours it becomes superinfected with bacterial flora (secondary bacterial peritonitis).
  • gastric acid with pH <4 induces necrosis and fibrinous exudate; the inflammatory response causes flat abdomen and intense pain.
  • chemical peritonitis explains why the initial pain is more intense than the physical finding in early cases; fever and leukocytosis appear with bacterial contamination.
  • Initial treatment includes intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering gram-negative and anaerobic) before surgery.

items.title: exploratory laparotomy
items.contentHtml:
Emergency surgery: exploratory laparotomy

  • Exploratory laparotomy is the treatment of choice for perforated peptic ulcer; Laparoscopic surgery is an alternative in centers with experience and stable patients.
  • The indication is urgent; Delay >24 hours from perforation increases mortality significantly (up to 30-50%).
  • The examination should include inspection of the anterior surface of the duodenal bulb and the lesser gastric curvature; Abundant peritoneal lavage is performed with saline solution.
  • In patients with hemodynamic instability or fecaloid peritonitis, laparotomy is mandatory; emergency surgery should not be delayed by imaging studies if the diagnosis is clear.

items.title: Peritoneal lavage and primary closure
items.contentHtml:
Peritoneal lavage and primary closure

  • Peritoneal lavage with abundant saline solution (minimum 10 liters) reduces the bacterial load and fibrinous material; It is performed before closure.
  • Primary closure of the perforation with sutures (simple or in duodenal ulcers it is not necessary.
  • Peritoneal lavage can be combined with primary closure and omentum patch (Graham technique) to reinforce the suture and prevent leaks.

items.title: graham patch
items.contentHtml:
Graham patch

  • The Graham patch consists of placing an omentum patch over the perforation and fixing it with tension-free sutures; It is the most used technique for perforated duodenal ulcers.
  • The omentum is sutured with loose stitches that pass through both edges of the perforation and the omentum; The objective is to plug without stenosis of the lumen.
  • Indicated in perforations <2 cm, with clean edges and without signs of malignancy; in gastric perforations, it should be biopsied before the patch.
  • In large perforations or with tissue loss, gastrectomy or modified Graham procedure may be required; The decision depends on the patient's condition.

items.title: Risk triad
items.contentHtml:
Triad: ulcer, NSAIDs, smoking

  • The triad: ulcer, NSAIDs, smoking describes the classic risk factors for peptic ulcer perforation; the use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and smoking increase the incidence of complications.
  • NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase-1 and reduce the production of prostaglandins, reducing mucus and bicarbonate; the risk of perforation is dose-dependent.
  • Smoking delays ulcer healing and increases acid secretion; the risk is multiplied if it is combined with NSAIDs.
  • In patients with peptic ulcer who require NSAIDs, a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) should be prescribed as prophylaxis; Eradication of Helicobacter pylori reduces the risk of relapse.

items.foco: H. pylori as the main etiological factor
items.title: Helicobacter pylori
items.contentHtml:
Helicobacter pylori

  • Helicobacter pylori is the main etiological factor of peptic ulcer; It is present in 90% of duodenal ulcers and 70% of gastric ulcers.
  • Chronic infection causes antral gastritis, hypergastrinemia and increased acid secretion; colonization of the duodenum with gastric metaplasia predisposes to ulcer.
  • The eradication of H. pylori reduces the ulcer recurrence rate from 60-90% to <5%; It is confirmed with a breath test or fecal antigen at 4 weeks.
  • In acute perforation, the rapid urease test can give false negatives; It is recommended to take a biopsy for culture or histological test, and treat if positive.

items.title: plain x-ray
items.contentHtml:
Plain x-ray: subdiaphragmatic air

  • The plain x-ray of the chest in standing position is the first imaging test in case of suspected perforation; looks for subdiaphragmatic air under the diaphragmatic domes.
  • The subdiaphragmatic air is seen as a radiolucent crescent-shaped image between the diaphragm and the liver or stomach; Its presence confirms pneumoperitoneum.
  • The sensitivity of plain radiography is limited: in small perforations or with little air, it may be normal; computed tomography has sensitivity >95%.
  • If the x-ray is negative but clinical suspicion is high, abdominal computed tomography with oral and intravenous contrast should be requested; Surgery should not be delayed.

items.foco: High mortality if delay is greater than 24 hours
items.title: Mortality and delay
items.contentHtml:
High mortality if delay greater than 24 hours

  • The mortality of perforated peptic ulcer is <5% if surgery is performed within the first 6 hours; It amounts to 30-50% if the delay is >24 hours.
  • The delay greater than 24 hours is associated with bacterial peritonitis, sepsis and multiple organ failure; advanced age and comorbidities increase the risk.
  • The Boey scale (presence of shock, major comorbidity and delay >24 hours) predicts mortality: 0 criteria = 0-1%, 3 criteria = >50%.
  • Aggressive preoperative resuscitation with fluids, antibiotics and analgesia should not delay surgery; The goal is to operate <24 hours from the onset of symptoms.
